text: Every model built in this chapter so far has used table or view, the defaults. That was the right choice for Lessons 2 through 4. The final orders fact model is different, by design, because of what it sits on top of.

Lesson 1 established the fact that matters here: raw_orders gets new rows every day the shop is open, not a one-time load. A table-materialized fact model would re-scan and re-transform every order ever placed, every single run, just to pick up today's rows.

This isn't a bug. A table-materialized version of this model would still produce the right numbers, forever. What breaks is cost: almost all of that rebuild time gets spent re-deriving rows that were already correct yesterday.

Picture it live for a year. The useful new work each run does — processing one day's new orders — stays roughly constant. The total work a table rebuild does keeps climbing, because it re-derives all the old, already-correct rows every single time.
Next lesson: building the incremental orders model, with is_incremental() doing exactly what Lesson 4's model doesn't need yet.
